Your action: anticipate this on every admission—consider lowering the olanzapine dose when a heavy smoker quits, and conversely expect levels to drop and possible relapse if he resumes smoking at discharge. It's the smoke, not nicotine, so patches don't cause the interaction. Bottom line: Smoking cessation raises olanzapine and clozapine levels via loss of CYP1A2 induction—adjust the dose.

stem: Which of the following parent behaviors is most important to a toddler's language development?
scenario: At a well-child visit, parents of a quiet 2-year-old ask how to boost his vocabulary, suggesting flashcards and drilling. You counsel that the strongest driver of toddler language is rich, frequent conversation, including narrating daily activities and thinking aloud, rather than explicit definitions or commands. You coach them to talk through cooking, dressing, and errands, label objects in context, and respond to the child's babble as if it were conversation. This guidance is concrete anticipatory care that supports expressive and receptive language development. Bottom line: Frequent conversation and thinking aloud, not drilling, best builds a toddler's language.

stem: Which of the following parent behaviors is most important to a toddler's language development?
scenario: A worried mother in your outpatient clinic asks how to boost her quiet 22-month-old's vocabulary, mentioning flashcards and drilling word definitions. Rather than endorsing rote definition or loud, slow repetition, you coach her on the highest-yield strategy: rich, frequent back-and-forth conversation and narrating her own actions aloud ('Now I'm pouring the milk into your cup'). This dialogic, language-immersive input drives toddler expressive development far more than explicit teaching. You frame it as a no-cost behavioral intervention and screen for hearing or autism if delays persist. Bottom line: Frequent conversation and thinking aloud, not drilling definitions, best fuels a toddler's language development.

stem: The impaired physician who fails to obtain or benefit from treatment may require the services of an administrative psychiatrist skilled in performing fitness-for-duty evaluations. In these situations, the administrative psychiatrist:
scenario: Your program director asks you to evaluate a senior resident whose colleagues report slurred speech and missed handoffs. You're tempted to frame yourself as the resident's advocate and promise everything stays between you two. Stop. In a fitness-for-duty evaluation you are an administrative psychiatrist, not a treating physician, and the usual confidentiality contract does not apply: your findings go to the referring institution. Before the interview, you explicitly tell the resident there is no doctor-patient relationship and that your report will be shared. That warning protects them, protects the public, and keeps your assessment ethically clean. You assess fitness; you do not treat or advocate. Bottom line: In a fitness-for-duty eval you serve the institution, so disclose the limits of confidentiality up front.

stem: The impaired physician who fails to obtain or benefit from treatment may require the services of an administrative psychiatrist skilled in performing fitness-for-duty evaluations. In these situations, the administrative psychiatrist:
scenario: Your hospital's physician health committee asks you to do a fitness-for-duty evaluation on a surgeon whose colleagues report slurred speech and missed cases. Before you start, you make clear to the surgeon that this is not treatment and that your findings go to the committee, your client. When he later asks you to keep his admission of opioid use private, you explain you cannot, because in an administrative evaluation you are not bound by the usual treatment confidentiality. You document the limits of confidentiality up front, obtain acknowledgment, and report your safety-relevant findings to the requesting body rather than to the physician alone. Bottom line: In fitness-for-duty work you serve the organization, so warn the evaluee that ordinary confidentiality does not apply.

stem: A 22-year-old female is hospitalized with severe paranoia and hallucinations. During the review of systems, she acknowledges a history of acute abdominal pain, particularly during menstruation. Physical examination reveals reduced strength in the proximal upper and lower extremities and reduced tendon reflexes. Which of the following laboratory values is likely to be elevated and would explain her symptoms?
scenario: On C-L consult you see a young woman admitted to medicine for unexplained psychosis. The primary team is leaning toward a primary psychiatric diagnosis, but you notice the cluster that does not fit: recurrent severe abdominal pain timed to menses, proximal weakness, and diminished reflexes. That neuro-visceral-psychiatric triad should stop you before you reach for an antipsychotic. You recommend a spot urine for porphobilinogen and ALA, and you flag that certain psychotropics and starvation can precipitate attacks. Confirming acute intermittent porphyria changes management entirely: IV hemin, dextrose loading, pain control, and scrupulous avoidance of porphyrinogenic drugs. Bottom line: Psychosis plus colicky abdominal pain and neuropathy means check urine porphobilinogen before blaming a primary psychiatric illness.

stem: A 22-year-old female is hospitalized with severe paranoia and hallucinations. During the review of systems she acknowledges a history of acute abdominal pain, particularly during menstruation. Physical examination reveals reduced strength in the proximal upper and lower extremities and reduced tendon reflexes. Which of the following laboratory values is likely to be elevated and would explain her symptoms?
scenario: A 22-year-old woman is admitted to your unit with new paranoia and hallucinations, and the team is leaning toward primary psychosis. On review of systems she mentions recurrent severe abdominal pain that flares around her menses, and your exam finds proximal weakness with reduced reflexes. That triad of neuropsychiatric symptoms, abdominal pain, and a motor neuropathy should stop you before you reflexively start an antipsychotic, since many of those drugs can precipitate attacks. You order a spot urine porphobilinogen, which is elevated in acute intermittent porphyria, and you avoid porphyrinogenic medications while giving IV glucose and hemin. Bottom line: Psychosis plus abdominal pain plus neuropathy should trigger a urine porphobilinogen test.

stem: The clock drawing in the image below is consistent with a lesion in which of the following areas of the brain?
scenario: During a bedside cognitive exam, your 68-year-old patient draws a clock with all the numbers crammed into one half of the circle, neglecting the left side. You recognize this visuospatial deficit and hemineglect as pointing to a parietal lobe lesion, often right parietal. This finding redirects your workup: you order neuroimaging looking for a right-hemisphere stroke or mass, perform a careful neglect and constructional-apraxia exam, and avoid attributing the picture to purely psychiatric causes. The clock-drawing test thus becomes a quick localizing tool that changes your differential and urgency. Bottom line: Spatial distortion and neglect on clock drawing localize to the parietal lobe.

stem: The clock drawing in the image below is consistent with a lesion in which of the following areas of the brain?
scenario: On a stroke C-L consult, you screen a patient with a clock drawing and notice the numbers crowded to one side with the left half neglected and spatial distortions. You recognize this constructional and hemispatial pattern points to parietal lobe (often right parietal) dysfunction rather than the planning failures you'd attribute to frontal disease. You document the visuospatial deficit, flag likely hemineglect for the team and PT/OT, and make sure the bedside and meal tray are arranged on the intact side to keep the patient safe. The clock becomes a quick, repeatable bedside localizer that guides rehab and fall precautions. Bottom line: Visuospatial and hemineglect errors on the clock drawing localize to the parietal lobe.

stem: The consultation-liaison psychiatrist evaluates a 54-year-old patient with end-stage breast cancer. The patient was previously very optimistic and energetic but has recently been told that the treatment protocol had failed and only palliative care was recommended. Since that time the patient has appeared depressed, and the team is concerned that she is suicidal. On interview, the patient is initially pleasant and able to amiably discuss neutral topics. When the subject shifts to her illness, the patient becomes tearful and expresses a crushing feeling of hopelessness about the future. She denies any plan to hurt herself, saying, "What's the point? I'm going to die soon anyway, but I would rather God just took me and didn't draw this out." Which of the following would be the best initial approach to this patient?
scenario: As the C-L psychiatrist you see a 54-year-old with end-stage breast cancer who became tearful and hopeless after learning treatment failed; the team fears she is suicidal. On interview she denies any plan and says she wishes God would simply take her without prolonging things, a passive wish reflecting demoralization rather than major depression or active suicidality. Your best first move is to validate her grief as a normal, expectable response to an overwhelming loss, building alliance before assessing whether a treatable depressive syndrome is also present. You avoid a knee-jerk locked-unit transfer or premature medication. Bottom line: Demoralization at end of life calls first for empathic validation, not reflexive hospitalization or diagnosis of major depression.

stem: The consultation-liaison psychiatrist evaluates a 54-year-old patient with end-stage breast cancer. The patient was previously very optimistic and energetic, but has recently been told that the treatment protocol had failed and only palliative care was recommended. Since that time the patient has appeared depressed, and the team is concerned that she is suicidal. On interview, the patient is initially pleasant and able to amiably discuss neutral topics. When the subject shifts to her illness, the patient becomes tearful and expresses a crushing feeling of hopelessness about the future. She denies any plan to hurt herself, saying, "What's the point? I'm going to die soon anyway, but I would rather God just took me and didn't draw this out." Which of the following would be the best initial approach to this patient?
scenario: The oncology team pages your C-L service: a 54-year-old with end-stage breast cancer just learned treatment failed and seems depressed and possibly suicidal. At bedside she chats pleasantly until the topic turns to her illness, then becomes tearful and hopeless, saying she'd rather God took her than draw this out, but denies any plan to act. Before reaching for an antidepressant or transfer, your best initial move is to validate her response as a normal reaction to an overwhelming situation, building the alliance and allowing fuller assessment. You distinguish demoralization from major depression and avoid pathologizing existential distress. Bottom line: With terminal illness and hopelessness but no plan, validate first, then assess for treatable depression.

stem: Which of the following statistics measures the magnitude of difference between two intervention groups?
scenario: At journal club a resident excitedly reports a trial where the new antidepressant beat placebo with p less than 0.001 and wants to switch patients. You slow them down: the p-value tells you the difference is unlikely due to chance, but not how big or clinically meaningful it is. For magnitude you look at the effect size (for example Cohen's d or the standardized mean difference). A tiny effect size can still be statistically significant in a large trial. The resident reframes their appraisal around effect size before changing practice. Bottom line: The p-value shows whether a difference exists; effect size tells you how large and clinically meaningful it is.

stem: Which of the following statistics measures the magnitude of difference between two intervention groups?
scenario: You are on the residency journal club presenting a new antidepressant trial. It reports a tiny but statistically significant p-value, and a colleague concludes the drug is clearly superior. You push back: the p-value only tells you the difference is unlikely due to chance, not how large or clinically meaningful it is. You point the group to the effect size, which actually quantifies the magnitude of difference between the two groups. The effect size turns out to be small, so you frame the result as real but modest when deciding whether to change practice. Bottom line: A significant p-value says a difference exists; the effect size tells you whether it is big enough to matter.

stem: When a patient in alcohol withdrawal is experiencing hallucinations, the presence of which of the following would suggest a diagnosis of alcohol hallucinosis rather than delirium tremens?
scenario: On overnight call you evaluate an alcohol-withdrawing patient reporting vivid auditory hallucinations. The pivotal bedside question is his sensorium: he is alert, fully oriented, and tracking the conversation with normal vitals. That clear sensorium points to alcohol hallucinosis rather than delirium tremens, which is defined by clouded consciousness, disorientation, and autonomic instability. You still treat withdrawal with benzodiazepines and monitor, but you recognize this is not the life-threatening DTs picture and may add an antipsychotic for the hallucinations while keeping a low threshold to escalate if his mental status clouds. Bottom line: A clear sensorium distinguishes alcohol hallucinosis from the delirium and autonomic chaos of DTs.

stem: When a patient in alcohol withdrawal is experiencing hallucinations, the presence of which of the following would suggest a diagnosis of alcohol hallucinosis rather than delirium tremens?
scenario: Two patients on your detox unit are hallucinating. One is febrile, tachycardic, tremulous, and disoriented, while the other vividly describes voices but is fully alert, oriented, and tracking the conversation normally. The key bedside discriminator is sensorium: alcoholic hallucinosis features a clear sensorium with relatively stable vitals, whereas delirium tremens is a hyperadrenergic delirium with clouded consciousness and autonomic instability. This distinction drives disposition and risk: the DTs patient needs aggressive benzodiazepine loading and close monitoring for a life-threatening course, while hallucinosis is lower-acuity. Bottom line: A clear sensorium points to alcoholic hallucinosis rather than delirium tremens, so always assess orientation and autonomic status.

stem: An effectiveness study differs from an efficacy study in that it includes which of the following?
scenario: A resident presents a tightly controlled efficacy trial of an antidepressant and asks why your messy clinic patients respond less impressively. You distinguish efficacy from effectiveness: efficacy studies use random assignment, blinding, restrictive inclusion criteria, and circumscribed populations to prove a drug can work under ideal conditions, while effectiveness studies test real-world conditions, with comorbidities, adherence problems, and broad populations like STAR*D or CATIE. Knowing the difference lets you weigh whether trial results generalize to the patient in front of you. You cite effectiveness data when counseling about realistic outcomes. Bottom line: Effectiveness studies test treatments under real-world conditions, so they generalize better than tightly controlled efficacy trials.

stem: An effectiveness study differs from an efficacy study in that it includes which of the following?
scenario: A resident asks why a tightly controlled antidepressant efficacy trial does not match what she sees in clinic. You explain the efficacy-effectiveness distinction. Efficacy studies use restrictive inclusion criteria, narrow populations, and ideal conditions to prove a drug can work. Effectiveness studies test the drug under real-world conditions, with comorbidities, adherence problems, and messy patients like hers. When choosing literature to guide a complex clinic patient, you weight effectiveness data, such as STAR*D, more heavily because it reflects who you actually treat. This keeps your expectations realistic and your recommendations grounded. Bottom line: Effectiveness studies test treatments under real-world conditions, so lean on them when generalizing to your everyday patients.

stem: The physiologic changes during REM sleep include increased eye movements, decreased muscle tone, and which of the following?
scenario: Reading a sleep study on a patient with suspected REM behavior disorder, you note the autonomic findings. During REM sleep, alongside rapid eye movements and skeletal muscle atonia, the heart rate and blood pressure become increased and variable, and breathing is irregular. This matters clinically. The autonomic surges of REM help explain why cardiovascular events and arrhythmias cluster in the early morning when REM is densest, and why nightmares and panic-like awakenings emerge from this stage. Recognizing normal REM physiology keeps you from misreading expected tachycardia as pathology. Bottom line: REM sleep features muscle atonia but increased, variable heart rate and autonomic activity.

stem: The physiologic changes during REM sleep include increased eye movements, decreased muscle tone and which of the following?
scenario: Reading a sleep study with the tech, you note that during REM epochs the patient shows muscle atonia and bursts of eye movement, but his heart rate and blood pressure become irregular and surge upward, and breathing turns erratic. This autonomic instability matters clinically: REM is when nocturnal angina, arrhythmias, and apnea-related desaturations cluster, which is why a cardiac patient's worst events often hit in the early morning REM-rich hours. Understanding that REM drives sympathetic surges helps you counsel patients and interpret why events are timed as they are. Bottom line: REM sleep brings autonomic activation with increased, variable heart rate despite skeletal muscle atonia.

stem: Which of the following abnormalities of speech or language is a patient with autism spectrum disorder most likely to demonstrate?
scenario: In clinic a school refers a verbal 8-year-old you're evaluating for autism. His grammar and vocabulary are fine, but his speech is flat and sing-song, with odd stress and little melodic variation, and he misses your tone when you joke. That impaired prosody, the social-communication music of language rather than its mechanics, is a classic autism finding, distinct from aphasia or dyslexia. You document it as part of the social-communication criteria, fold it into your diagnostic formulation, and use it to justify a speech-language referral targeting pragmatic and prosodic skills, not just articulation. It also guides parents on reading his intent. Bottom line: In autism, listen for impaired prosody, the social melody of speech, not classic language errors.

stem: Which of the following abnormalities of speech or language is a patient with autism spectrum disorder most likely to demonstrate?
scenario: Evaluating a verbal 8-year-old for possible autism, you listen carefully to how he speaks, not just what he says. His words are grammatically intact but flat and sing-song, with odd stress and little emotional inflection, classic impaired prosody. This abnormal melody and rhythm of speech is among the most characteristic language features in autism spectrum disorder, distinct from aphasia or dyslexia. Noting it supports your diagnosis, guides referral for speech-language therapy targeting social communication, and helps you counsel teachers that his monotone is part of the condition, not rudeness. Bottom line: Impaired prosody, the abnormal melody and rhythm of speech, is a hallmark language feature of autism.

stem: Because it acts as both an inducer and substrate of CYP3A4, which of the following medications might require a dose increase after several weeks to maintain steady-state blood levels?
scenario: You start a patient on carbamazepine for bipolar disorder and obtain a good therapeutic level at three weeks. A month later they relapse and the level has dropped despite perfect adherence. The explanation is autoinduction: carbamazepine is both a substrate and inducer of CYP3A4, so it accelerates its own metabolism over the first few weeks. Anticipating this, you plan to recheck levels and increase the dose after several weeks to maintain steady state. It also reminds you to watch interactions, since carbamazepine lowers levels of many co-prescribed drugs like oral contraceptives. Bottom line: Carbamazepine autoinduces CYP3A4, so levels fall over weeks and the dose usually needs increasing.

stem: Because it acts as both an inducer and substrate of CYP3A4, which of the following medications might require a dose increase after several weeks to maintain steady-state blood levels?
scenario: You start a patient on carbamazepine for bipolar disorder and check a level two weeks in that looks therapeutic. A month later the patient relapses and the repeat level has dropped despite perfect adherence. You recognize autoinduction: carbamazepine is both a substrate and an inducer of CYP3A4, so it ramps up its own metabolism over the first few weeks, lowering steady-state levels. Anticipating this, you plan to recheck levels and increase the dose after several weeks rather than assuming nonadherence. Bottom line: Carbamazepine autoinduces CYP3A4, so expect falling levels over the first weeks and proactively recheck and uptitrate.

stem: A 38-year-old female patient is noted to have continuously active muscle spasm of the proximal limbs and axial trunk. Lumbar lordosis becomes exaggerated while walking. Electromyography (EMG) shows no evidence of distal motor nerve abnormality. Antiglutamic acid decarboxylase antibodies are present in serum. Which of the following syndromes is the most likely diagnosis?
scenario: A resident evaluates a patient with months of progressive truncal stiffness, exaggerated lordosis, and sudden painful spasms triggered by unexpected noise. Strength and sensation are largely preserved between spasms, and testing detects anti-GAD antibodies. The resident recognizes a stiff-person-spectrum presentation and involves neurology while considering mimics such as dystonia, myelopathy, parkinsonism, tetanus, functional neurologic symptoms, and peripheral nerve hyperexcitability. EMG assessment for continuous motor-unit activity and evaluation for associated autoimmune disease or relevant malignancy may refine the diagnosis. Treatment planning commonly combines symptomatic enhancement of inhibitory signaling with specialist-directed immunotherapy when appropriate. Bottom line: Axial rigidity, stimulus-triggered spasms, lumbar lordosis, and anti-GAD antibodies strongly indicate stiff-person syndrome.

stem: A 24-year-old female patient presents to the emergency department after making ten horizontal, superficial cuts in her left wrist. The patient asserts having no intention to die at the time, but simply wanted “to feel something.” On further questioning, it becomes apparent that the patient frequently cuts and burns herself when she is under stress, stating that “life is just too hard sometimes; it might be easier if I were dead.” The decision to admit this patient to the psychiatric hospital would be most strongly supported by the presence of which of the following in the patient’s history?
scenario: In the emergency department, a resident assesses a patient with chronic cutting who currently denies intent to die. The resident does not equate denial of intent with absence of risk. The interview addresses recent alcohol use, current intoxication, withdrawal risk, access to lethal means, suicidal planning, prior attempts, agitation, supports, and the patient's ability to participate in a collaborative safety plan. If recent alcohol abuse accompanies impaired judgment, escalating self-harm, or inability to ensure safety, a higher level of care may be indicated. Disposition remains individualized and should not automatically hospitalize every patient with borderline traits or superficial injuries. Bottom line: Substance-related disinhibition can convert chronic self-harm and passive death wishes into an acute safety emergency.

stem: A 72-year-old patient with early dementia is paranoid and has visual hallucinations. The patient’s caretaker reports that the patient seems lightheaded and is socially inappropriate. After 2 days of treatment with risperidone 0.25 mg, the caretaker reports that the patient is more confused and sedated. On examination, the patient has new-onset rigidity. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the patient’s psychosis?
scenario: An older adult with cognitive decline is admitted for distressing visual hallucinations and suspiciousness. Before labeling the symptoms as a primary psychotic disorder, the resident obtains collateral history about cognitive fluctuations, dream enactment, falls, autonomic symptoms, and spontaneous motor slowing or rigidity. The combination of visual hallucinations and parkinsonism raises concern for Lewy body disease. If behavioral treatment is necessary, the team first looks for delirium, pain, infection, medication effects, and environmental triggers. It uses nonpharmacologic strategies when possible and is especially cautious with dopamine-blocking drugs because severe sensitivity reactions can occur. Bottom line: Visual hallucinations plus parkinsonism and antipsychotic sensitivity strongly suggest Lewy body disease.

stem: A 21-year-old male patient is dropped off at an emergency department (ED). The patient is agitated, believes computers in the ED are flashing messages at him, and says “I need my knife to protect myself.” Which of the following substances is most likely to be found on urine toxicology?
scenario: An emergency resident evaluates an agitated young adult who reports that electronic devices are communicating threats and requests a weapon for protection. Staff first use a low-stimulation setting, verbal de-escalation, and safety precautions while assessing vital signs, temperature, glucose, trauma, delirium, and access to weapons. History and toxicology testing are adjuncts; neither replaces clinical assessment. Stimulant-related psychosis becomes more likely when paranoia follows recent stimulant use with insomnia, tachycardia, diaphoresis, or repetitive behavior. Persistent symptoms after expected intoxication resolution should prompt reassessment for a primary psychotic, mood, neurologic, or other substance-induced disorder. Bottom line: Marked agitation with paranoid ideas of reference makes stimulant intoxication a leading consideration.

stem: A 54-year-old patient suffers an acute bleed from a gastric ulcer which requires emergency surgical treatment. Thirty hours postoperatively, 36 hours since the bleed, the patient becomes confused and agitated, while being transferred from the ICU to the floor. The patient appears to be responding to auditory and visual hallucinations, and suffers a generalized tonic-clonic seizure. This clinical state is most likely which of the following?
scenario: A hospitalized patient becomes tremulous, agitated, disoriented, and visually hallucinating after emergency surgery. The resident treats this as a medical emergency: assess airway and vital signs, evaluate for seizures and alternative causes of delirium, obtain collateral substance-use history, and involve the appropriate medical team. Alcohol-withdrawal protocols commonly use sedative treatment and close monitoring; thiamine is considered in patients at risk of deficiency. The resident does not assume postoperative confusion is solely anesthetic-related. Severe agitation, perceptual disturbance, and seizure require rapid escalation and a broad delirium workup while withdrawal is treated. Bottom line: Delirium with hallucinations and seizures after abrupt alcohol cessation is delirium tremens until proven otherwise.

stem: A 29-year-old male patient with schizophrenia has been hospitalized with delusions of persecution eight times in the past 14 months, after stopping medication. The patient has been unable to stay in a board and care facility for more than 3 continuous weeks, since he becomes paranoid and leaves, preferring to stay on the street, eating mostly out of garbage cans. The patient’s parents report being unable to continue to support their son if he will not take his medication consistently. Which of the following interventions would be most appropriate to decrease this patient’s risk of future hospitalizations?
scenario: A patient with schizophrenia has repeated admissions after stopping medication, sleeps outdoors, and leaves residential settings because of paranoia. At discharge planning, the resident recognizes that a standard clinic referral is unlikely to meet the patient’s needs. The team refers to ACT, coordinates with housing and benefits services, involves family with permission, and develops a practical outreach plan for missed visits and medication support. The ACT model can meet patients in community settings, maintain frequent contact, and integrate psychiatric and social interventions. Medication selection remains important, including consideration of long-acting formulations when appropriate, but service intensity and continuity are central to reducing the revolving-door pattern. Bottom line: ACT is indicated when severe mental illness is paired with recurrent hospitalization and failure to engage in conventional outpatient care.

stem: A 72-year-old patient is referred for psychiatric consultation by an ophthalmologist, for evaluation of visual hallucinations. The patient is legally blind from macular degeneration, but is in otherwise good health and has no other psychiatric history. The patient reports experiencing well-formed visual hallucinations of people and animals ever since the vision loss became severe. The hallucinations are not accompanied by any other symptoms. The patient reports knowing that the hallucinations do not represent real stimuli. Auditory hallucinations, delusional beliefs, mood disturbance, or other psychiatric symptoms are denied. The patient has no apparent cognitive problems, and continues to work as an attorney. Mental status examination is unremarkable except for the visual hallucinations. This patient’s visual hallucinations are most likely due to:
scenario: An ophthalmology clinic requests psychiatric input for an older patient with macular degeneration who describes seeing small animals in the home. The resident asks about visual loss, insight, timing, medications, cognition, sleep, delirium symptoms, mood, and hallucinations in other modalities. Preserved orientation and functioning, absence of delusional conviction, and awareness that images are unreal support Charles Bonnet syndrome. The resident explains the likely sensory-deprivation mechanism in non-stigmatizing language and coordinates medical evaluation if new neurologic, cognitive, or systemic symptoms are present. Reassurance alone may reduce distress, while management should reflect severity and the broader medical context. Bottom line: Formed visual hallucinations with insight after vision loss are classic for Charles Bonnet syndrome.

stem: A 32-year-old patient presents with new-onset panic attacks, which have been occurring at least weekly for the past month. Physical examination and laboratory workup is negative for a medical cause and panic disorder is diagnosed. The patient is in otherwise good health, and has no history of other psychiatric or substance-related disorders. Which of the following is the most appropriate first-line treatment for this disorder?
scenario: A resident evaluates a patient with recurrent unexpected panic attacks, negative medical evaluation, and avoidance of places where attacks occurred. The resident offers panic-focused cognitive-behavioral therapy and an SSRI such as fluoxetine, explaining that benefit is gradual and transient early jitteriness can occur. Follow-up assesses adherence, activation, suicidality, substance use, sleep, and ongoing avoidance. The resident reinforces exposure-based behavioral strategies and avoids presenting medication as the sole intervention. If symptoms are atypical, new, or accompanied by concerning physical findings, the differential is revisited rather than attributing everything to panic. Bottom line: SSRIs and CBT are first-line treatments for panic disorder; fluoxetine is the SSRI option here.

stem: An 85-year-old patient with a history of dementia is admitted from a nursing home for agitation, being more confused than usual, and screaming “fire” whenever the light next to the bed is turned on. Which of the following is the most appropriate next action?
scenario: A nursing-home resident with established dementia becomes suddenly frightened, screams when a bedside light is turned on, and is more disoriented than usual. The psychiatry resident distinguishes chronic cognitive impairment from an acute fluctuating change and reviews vital signs, medications, hydration, pain, constipation, urinary symptoms, and the neurologic examination. Basic medical evaluation, including the keyed urinalysis, is initiated while staff reduce overstimulation and ensure safety. The resident avoids reflexively treating the behavior with a benzodiazepine because it may worsen delirium. If focal deficits, head trauma, persistent unexplained symptoms, or seizure concern emerges, targeted neurologic testing follows. Bottom line: sudden behavioral change in dementia requires a delirium and reversible-cause workup first.

stem: A psychiatrist is consulted regarding an 88-year-old patient with dementia. The psychiatrist is asked to assess the patient’s competence to make medical decisions, and to determine the best treatment for the patient’s agitation. The patient has a durable power of attorney for healthcare. If the psychiatrist finds that the patient is incompetent to make medical decisions, treatment recommendations will have to be approved by the:
scenario: On a consultation-liaison service, an 88-year-old patient with dementia cannot understand the proposed medication’s purpose, risks, or alternatives and cannot communicate a stable choice. The resident documents a decision-specific capacity assessment and confirms that a durable health-care power of attorney is active and identifies a particular person. The team then discusses the proposed agitation plan with that assigned surrogate, seeking a decision guided by the patient’s known values and preferences. The resident still involves the patient to the greatest extent possible and reassesses capacity if mental status changes. Emergency stabilization follows local law and hospital policy. Bottom line: for an incapacitated patient, the designated health-care surrogate is the usual authorized decision maker.

stem: A 62-year-old patient is being evaluated for frequent falls without loss of consciousness. The patient has rigidity and hallucinations. The patient has had three episodes of auditory and visual hallucinations that resolved without sequelae. Which of the following medications is likely to aggravate the patient’s condition?
scenario: An older inpatient has fluctuating attention, visual hallucinations, bradykinesia, and repeated falls. Staff request a standing antipsychotic because the hallucinations are frightening. The resident first evaluates for delirium, pain, infection, medication effects, and environmental triggers. If treatment is necessary, the team uses nonpharmacologic measures and coordinates with neurology or geriatrics, recognizing that conventional dopamine-blocking antipsychotics can markedly worsen motor and cognitive status in suspected Lewy body dementia. Fall precautions and medication reconciliation are also essential. Bottom line: Avoid or use exceptional caution with risperidone in Lewy body dementia.

stem: A 42-year-old woman recently had an abdominal hysterectomy for endometriosis. On the fourth day after surgery, her meperidine prescription is changed from 75 mg IM q4h to 100 mg PO q4h. As a result, the woman reports inadequate pain relief, requests that the injections be resumed, and anxiously anticipates each analgesic dose. The consulting psychiatrist who examines her for iatrogenic addiction finds the patient to be very anxious, but she has no history of prior psychiatric disorder or substance abuse. The patient’s experience of pain most likely is due to:
scenario: A postoperative patient repeatedly asks for an opioid after a route change and is described as drug seeking. The clinician first reviews the medication record, route conversion, timing, pain syndrome, and nonopioid options with the surgical team. Requests for analgesia can reflect an inadequate regimen rather than addiction, while sedation, delirium, respiratory depression, and other opioid adverse effects still require monitoring. Current prescribing should favor safer analgesic alternatives to meperidine when possible and use local equianalgesic guidance rather than relying on the historical drug example. The patient should be addressed without moralizing or diagnostic assumptions. Bottom line: Before labeling a hospitalized patient as addicted, verify whether the route and dose provide adequate analgesia.

stem: A 73-year-old woman found on the floor at home seems unaware of her inability to use her left upper and lower extremities. Although her left arm is flaccid at her side, she denies that there is anything wrong. When she is asked to raise the left upper extremity, she raises the right one. When the psychiatrist lifts her left arm up and asks, “Whose arm is this?”, she responds, “Yours.” This type of behavior is most indicative of a lesion in the right:
scenario: A psychiatry resident is asked to assess a hospitalized patient who insists that nothing is wrong despite new left-sided weakness. On examination, the patient does not acknowledge the paretic arm and identifies it as someone else’s when it is placed in view. The resident recognizes that this is not simply psychological denial; it suggests a right parietal association-cortex syndrome and prompts urgent neurologic coordination if not already underway. The team also uses safety measures because neglect and unawareness increase fall and rehabilitation risks. Capacity assessment should account for the patient’s neurologically impaired appreciation of deficits. Bottom line: denial of contralateral paralysis with failure to recognize the limb localizes classically to the right parietal lobe.

stem: Which of the following is the most likely etiology of a posterior cerebral artery infarct in a 36-year-old woman with a history of migraine?
scenario: When a young woman with migraine has an ischemic stroke, obtain a precise medication history that includes contraceptive formulation, nicotine exposure, other vascular risks, and migraine-aura features. Migraine history alone does not establish a stroke mechanism, and focal neurologic symptoms should never be dismissed as anxiety or migraine without medical assessment. The neurologic and primary teams direct the etiologic workup and contraception plan; psychiatric clinicians can help clarify exposures, mood symptoms, and the impact of sudden illness. Estrogen exposure is clinically relevant but does not exclude cardiac, arterial, or hypercoagulable mechanisms. Bottom line: In a young patient with migraine and stroke, ask specifically about estrogen-containing contraception.

stem: A 59-year-old male physician consults a psychiatrist after being relieved of work duties at a hospital, because he presented for duty with alcohol on his breath, which was confirmed by a positive blood alcohol level. The patient endorses a few depressive symptoms of recent onset. He explains that he was an emergency medicine physician, and complains that, over the last year, he has been less tolerant of the change from day to night duty, where he has been feeling less alert and attentive. The patient reports using alcohol at such times to try to sleep during the day, and admits that he might have consumed it excessively for that purpose. The patient’s spouse expresses concern about the patient’s recent depressed mood and alcohol use. In addition to recommending abstinence from alcohol, the psychiatrist’s best next clinical step would be to:
scenario: A physician reports declining concentration after moving to overnight shifts and has begun drinking to sleep before daytime rest. Assess occupational safety, withdrawal risk, depressive symptoms, sleep duration, other substance use, and relevant fitness-for-duty processes while maintaining appropriate confidentiality boundaries. Coordinate with occupational health or a physician-health program when indicated, support abstinence, and seek a work schedule that permits stable sleep. Reassess mood symptoms after acute alcohol and sleep disruption are addressed, while not delaying care for severe depression, suicidality, or withdrawal. Bottom line: When alcohol use is tied to shift-work insomnia, change the schedule trigger while treating the substance use.

stem: Patients over 65 years old are less likely to tolerate higher doses of antipsychotic medications, due to which of the following factors?
scenario: An 80-year-old patient with delirium requires a short course of antipsychotic medication for dangerous agitation after nonpharmacologic measures are insufficient. The resident selects a low initial dose, reviews QT-prolonging and anticholinergic co-medications, checks relevant cardiac and metabolic risks, and reassesses daily for sedation, orthostasis, extrapyramidal effects, and ongoing need. A dose tolerated by a younger adult may produce excessive exposure or heightened sensitivity in this patient. The resident simultaneously treats the underlying cause of delirium rather than treating behavior alone. Bottom line: Reduced hepatic metabolism is one reason older adults often need lower antipsychotic doses and closer monitoring.

stem: A 55-year-old patient is brought to the emergency department by family members after the patient experienced an episode of amnesia and bewilderment lasting several hours. During the episode the patient’s behavior was normal, and the patient remained alert. The patient keeps asking questions about what is happening. Further workup provides no evidence for cerebrovascular disease or seizures. Which of the following would be the most appropriate step to take?
scenario: An older adult repeatedly asks why they are in the emergency department but remains cooperative, alert, and neurologically stable. Family reports sudden memory loss lasting hours without loss of identity or abnormal behavior. The clinician ensures appropriate evaluation for delirium, focal neurologic symptoms, seizure, substance effects, and metabolic causes. Once serious causes are excluded and the presentation supports transient global amnesia, the team provides a calm setting, repeats orientation information, observes recovery, and avoids unnecessary sedating medication. Family reassurance is important because the syndrome can be alarming. Bottom line: A classic, medically evaluated transient global amnesia episode is managed supportively rather than with psychotropics.

stem: A psychiatric consultation is requested for a 68-year-old patient who is depressed, following hip surgery. The patient is found to be withdrawn, lacks spontaneity, and looks blank. Examination shows dysarthria, psychomotor slowing, increased tone, hyperreflexia, trouble swallowing, and weakness. The patient admits to feeling frustrated. A magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan of the head is requested. Which of the following findings from the MRI is most likely?
scenario: After orthopedic surgery, an older adult appears depressed and minimally spontaneous. A consultation-liaison resident notices that the patient’s low output is accompanied by dysarthria, brisk reflexes, increased tone, dysphagia, and weakness. Rather than treating the presentation as uncomplicated major depression alone, the resident recommends neurologic evaluation and brain imaging while assessing delirium, medications, mood, and safety. Periventricular white-matter changes would support a vascular or subcortical contribution to executive slowing and affective change. The psychiatric formulation can then incorporate both emotional distress and brain-based impairment, with coordinated rehabilitation and medical management. Bottom line: Depression-like withdrawal plus pyramidal signs should prompt consideration of subcortical white-matter disease.

stem: A 41-year-old patient presents to the emergency department with a blood alcohol concentration (BAC) of 0.425 g/dL. The patient is stuporous, the pulse is 75, and the blood pressure is 110/70. There are no other drugs of abuse detected in the blood or urine. Which of the following would be the most immediate clinical concern?
scenario: In the emergency department, a stuporous patient with a very high BAC is placed on continuous monitoring. The resident promptly evaluates airway patency, respiratory rate and effort, oxygenation, ventilation, mental status, and evidence of trauma or co-ingestion. Because the patient may not reliably protect the airway, escalation for airway management is considered early while staff maintain aspiration precautions and obtain medical evaluation. A negative toxicology screen does not make severe ethanol intoxication benign. Once immediate physiologic stability is secured, the team can address withdrawal risk, substance-use treatment, and disposition. Bottom line: In severe alcohol intoxication with stupor, protect breathing first.

stem: After coronary bypass surgery, a 58-year-old man is noted to have some changes in mental status. On examination, it is noted that although his speech is fluent and he has excellent comprehension, he is unable to name fingers and body parts. When given commands involving right and left orientation, he often makes errors. He is also very frustrated by his inability to write down his thoughts and take notes, although he has good reading comprehension. He is unable to do calculations. The neurological examination is otherwise largely unremarkable. These findings are most consistent with:
scenario: Postoperative mental-status changes should not automatically be attributed to delirium. Brief bedside testing can reveal focal cortical signs: ask the patient to name fingers, distinguish right from left on self and examiner, write a sentence, and perform simple arithmetic. This constellation warrants urgent neurologic assessment for a dominant parietal lesion while clinicians also evaluate common postoperative contributors to confusion. Preserved fluent language does not exclude a clinically important stroke, and frustration may reflect awareness of a focal deficit rather than depression. Bottom line: Agraphia, acalculia, finger agnosia, and right-left confusion localize to the dominant angular gyrus.

stem: A 21-year-old patient experienced an acute illness that included hallucinations and delusions and met the criteria for the diagnosis of schizophrenia. As the condition evolved, the patient became largely mute, though would occasionally repeat the words or phrases of others in a parrot-like manner. This clinical picture is most compatible with which of the following subtypes of schizophrenia?
scenario: When an inpatient becomes nearly mute and repeats the interviewer’s words, assess for catatonia and additional signs such as staring, immobility, posturing, rigidity, withdrawal, echopraxia, and autonomic instability. Promptly consider medical, neurologic, mood, psychotic, and medication-related causes. Catatonia can impair eating, hydration, mobility, and safety, so it should not be dismissed as uncooperativeness. The item uses an obsolete schizophrenia-subtype classification, but the motor syndrome remains clinically urgent and cross-diagnostic. Bottom line: Mutism plus echolalia should trigger an assessment for catatonia and its underlying cause.

stem: A 28-year-old female patient with major depressive disorder and social phobia is undergoing interpersonal psychotherapy (IPT) to target long-standing social isolation. The patient reports being unhappy in a new job because coworkers go out to lunch together every day and do not invite her. Because of these worries, the patient has become more isolated for fear of embarrassing herself when interacting with others. In keeping with the principles of IPT, the psychiatrist should:
scenario: A clinician using IPT with a depressed patient maps the patient’s social network and identifies withdrawal after assumptions of rejection. Sessions focus on current interpersonal goals: identifying possible contacts, practicing direct invitations, exploring barriers to maintaining friendships, and reviewing specific interactions. The clinician links changes in isolation to mood symptoms without making the work primarily about disputing thoughts or reconstructing childhood conflict. Progress is monitored through symptom change and concrete interpersonal functioning, including contact frequency and relationship quality. Bottom line: IPT treats depression in part by improving present relationships and social support.

stem: A 56-year-old patient with diabetes and hypertension who smokes cigarettes complains of the acute onset of vertigo, nausea, vomiting, and unsteady gait. Examination shows decreased sensation to pin in the left side of the face, ataxia of the left upper and lower extremities, nystagmus, and hoarseness. As the patient walks, the patient veers to the left. The most likely diagnosis is:
scenario: A resident on a medical unit is asked to assess anxiety in a patient with sudden severe dizziness and vomiting. Rather than attributing the distress to panic, the resident notes nystagmus, new hoarseness, facial sensory asymmetry, and ipsilateral limb ataxia. These focal findings warrant immediate stroke-oriented evaluation and communication with the acute-care team. Continuous vertigo is not automatically peripheral; accompanying brainstem signs change the urgency and differential diagnosis. Bottom line: Acute vestibular symptoms plus focal neurologic deficits should raise concern for a posterior-circulation stroke, including lateral medullary stroke.

stem: A 4-year-old girl developed normally in the first 18 months of life, but afterwards developed decelerated head growth, loss of purposeful hand movements, midline upper extremity stereotypies (e.g., hand-wringing), severe psychomotor retardation and social withdrawal. These symptoms are characteristic of which of the following disorders?
scenario: A developmental consultation evaluates a young girl who developed typically during infancy but then lost purposeful hand skills and language while developing repetitive hand-wringing and gait impairment. The resident recognizes that regression, rather than delayed skill acquisition alone, is a critical diagnostic signal and arranges appropriate neurologic, developmental, and genetic evaluation. The team assesses for seizures, feeding difficulties, sleep disruption, scoliosis, and caregiver support needs as clinically indicated. The resident avoids mislabeling all social withdrawal as primary autism when a syndromic regression pattern is present. Bottom line: Regression in a young girl with loss of hand use and hand stereotypies strongly suggests Rett disorder.

stem: A 15-year-old child has history of seizures beginning at the age of 9 years, followed by prolonged motor or sensory deficits lasting days to weeks. The pattern of the seizures and the focal deficits has changed over time. The patient also has hemicranial headaches. There is no family history of similar symptoms. A recent magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan is shown above. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
scenario: A teenager has recurrent seizures, severe unilateral headaches, episodic focal deficits, and MRI abnormalities that change distribution over time. Rather than assuming repeated arterial strokes, the neurology and psychiatry teams consider a stroke-like mitochondrial syndrome such as MELAS and coordinate urgent neurologic assessment. The resident recognizes that psychiatric, cognitive, and mood symptoms can accompany neurologic disease but does not attribute fluctuating focal findings to a primary psychiatric disorder. Family history is reviewed carefully, but its absence is not used to exclude the diagnosis. Bottom line: Seizures, migraine-like headaches, and shifting stroke-like episodes in youth should prompt consideration of MELAS.

stem: A 61-year-old patient presents to the emergency department (ED) accompanied by family who report that the patient is unable to remember recent events. The patient's memory problems began 2 hours prior, and the patient was cognitively intact before this episode. The patient is alert, slightly anxious and frustrated, and repeatedly asks, "Why am I in the hospital, is someone sick?" This presentation is most consistent with a diagnosis of:
scenario: In the ED, a family reports that a 61-year-old repeatedly asks where they are and what happened, yet recognizes relatives, follows commands, and has normal speech and strength. The clinician obtains collateral history, establishes the time course, checks glucose, and performs a focused neurologic examination. Stroke, seizure, intoxication, delirium, and other dangerous mimics must be considered, especially if there are focal deficits, impaired consciousness, or atypical features. When the presentation remains classic and no red flags emerge, observation, reassurance, and appropriately targeted evaluation are reasonable. Bottom line: Sudden repetitive questioning with preserved alertness and no focal deficits strongly suggests transient global amnesia.

stem: A 35-year-old patient with a history of opioid and alcohol dependence presents to the emergency department complaining of tremulousness, anxiety, nausea and vomiting. The patient reports using large amounts of both heroin and alcohol the day prior. Which of the following would be the initial preferred medication to manage the patient's opioid withdrawal?
scenario: In the ED, a patient with opioid and alcohol dependence reports stopping or sharply reducing both substances and has nausea, vomiting, anxiety, and tremor. The clinician assesses airway, vital signs, mental status, intoxication, withdrawal severity, and risk for alcohol-withdrawal complications. Methadone can treat opioid withdrawal when clinically appropriate and permitted by the care setting’s protocols; contemporary pathways may instead use buprenorphine. Alcohol withdrawal requires its own evidence-based management and monitoring. After stabilization, the team should arrange linkage to continuing addiction treatment. Bottom line: The keyed answer is methadone for opioid withdrawal, while co-occurring alcohol withdrawal must be managed separately.

stem: The consultation/liaison psychiatrist is asked to see a 20-year-old patient with cancer pain who has been on a methadone maintenance program. The staff feels that the patient's requests for additional narcotics represent drug-seeking behavior. Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation?
scenario: An inpatient receiving methadone maintenance develops severe pain from advanced cancer. The clinician helps oncology and addiction teams recognize that the maintenance dose prevents withdrawal but is not equivalent to sustained cancer analgesia. The team verifies the outpatient regimen, continues it when appropriate, assesses pain and sedation repeatedly, and adds scheduled or short-acting analgesia based on response and opioid tolerance. Clear documentation and coordinated prescribing reduce stigma, conflict, and unsafe duplication. Nonopioid and nonpharmacologic measures can supplement, but should not replace adequate opioid analgesia when it is indicated. Bottom line: Maintenance methadone does not eliminate the need for appropriately titrated treatment of severe cancer pain.

stem: A 25-year-old patient reports having visual hallucinations described as similar to the wavy distortions produced by heat rising from asphalt and affecting the whole of both visual fields. These episodes of visual disturbance are accompanied by vertigo, dysarthria, and tingling in both hands and feet, and sometimes around both sides of the mouth followed by occipital headache. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this patient's symptoms?
scenario: In the emergency setting, a resident hears a history of transient vertigo, dysarthria, bilateral tingling, and visual phenomena followed by headache. The resident recognizes a possible migraine-with-brainstem-aura pattern but does not use that label to dismiss acute neurologic disease. Timing, reversibility, vascular risk factors, examination findings, and whether symptoms are new or different guide urgent neurologic evaluation. Document the sequence precisely: aura symptoms, duration, reversibility, then headache. Persistent deficits, unusual severity, or a changed pattern should prompt evaluation for stroke and other secondary causes. Bottom line: Reversible brainstem-type symptoms followed by migraine headache suggest migraine with brainstem aura, historically called basilar migraine.

stem: A 50-year-old patient with alcohol dependence is admitted to the emergency department (ED) for confusion, oculomotor disturbances, ataxia, and dysarthria. The first step in acute management of this patient's condition would be to administer which of the following medications?
scenario: In the emergency department, a patient with heavy alcohol use is confused, unsteady, and has abnormal eye movements. Treat suspected Wernicke encephalopathy promptly without waiting for the full triad or confirmatory testing. Order parenteral thiamine while evaluating nutrition, electrolytes, withdrawal risk, and other causes of altered mental status. If hypoglycemia is present, do not withhold glucose; administer thiamine immediately before or concomitantly. The classic findings are often incomplete, so maintain suspicion in malnourished or alcohol-dependent patients with compatible neurologic changes. Bottom line: Suspected Wernicke encephalopathy requires prompt parenteral thiamine, particularly when glucose is being given.

stem: A 79-year-old patient with a deteriorating mental state over a 3-week period has an exaggerated startle response with violent myoclonus that is elicited by turning on the room lights, speaking loudly, or touching the patient. Myoclonic jerks are also seen spontaneously. This clinical syndrome is strongly suggestive of which of the following etiologies?
scenario: An older adult develops rapidly worsening cognition over weeks, exaggerated startle, and recurrent myoclonic jerks. Do not prematurely attribute the presentation to delirium, depression, or a primary psychiatric disorder; arrange urgent neurologic and medical evaluation for rapidly progressive dementia. The differential includes toxic-metabolic, autoimmune, infectious, vascular, and prion causes, but striking stimulus-sensitive myoclonus raises the priority of a spongiform encephalopathy. If prion disease is evaluated, follow institutional guidance for appropriate specimen handling and procedural precautions. Bottom line: Rapid dementia with stimulus-sensitive myoclonus is a high-yield clue to prion-associated spongiform encephalopathy.

stem: A 27-year-old uninsured patient was hospitalized in an intensive care unit after a near-lethal overdose which followed the ending of a long-term intimate relationship. Family members had been told that the patient was going to visit friends out of town. The suicide note read, "I am sorry." The patient is medically ready for discharge, but is ambivalent about follow-up psychiatric care. The patient is noncommittal when asked about regretful feelings for surviving. Which of the following is the best approach for this patient?
scenario: After a medically serious intentional overdose, the consultation-liaison resident performs a full suicide assessment, seeks collateral information, reviews access to lethal means, and evaluates affect, intent, ambivalence, and capacity to participate in a safe disposition. Even if the patient now denies a specific plan, the recent near-lethal act and noncommittal response to survival warrant a higher level of psychiatric containment. Explain the recommendation respectfully and coordinate psychiatric transfer once medical clearance is complete, including family communication when appropriate. Begin discharge planning during admission. Bottom line: A recent near-lethal attempt with persistent ambivalence generally warrants inpatient psychiatric hospitalization.

stem: A 50-year-old fireman became clinically depressed after sustaining a myocardial infarction. The most appropriate medication to prescribe would be:
scenario: A resident evaluates depression emerging after myocardial infarction. The assessment includes whether symptoms meet criteria for a depressive disorder, suicidal thinking, delirium or cognitive impairment, medication effects, sleep, pain, and the patient’s understanding of the cardiac event. The resident coordinates with cardiology and primary care, reviews the medication list, and selects an antidepressant with favorable cardiovascular tolerability when medication is indicated. The team should monitor depressive symptoms and relevant medical parameters, encourage participation in rehabilitation when appropriate, and avoid assuming all post-infarction sadness is either normal grief or necessarily major depression. Treatment is individualized to the cardiac and psychiatric context. Bottom line: In depression after myocardial infarction, sertraline is a commonly preferred SSRI option among these choices.

stem: When an 80-year-old patient was admitted to a nursing home, an employee of the facility notified the patient about the state's laws on advance directives. During that session, the patient most likely received information about which of the following issues?
scenario: At nursing-home admission, a resident asks whether completing advance-directive paperwork means refusing life-sustaining treatment. The clinician should explain that the discussion is intended to provide information and preserve the resident's choices. The team can discuss documenting values and treatment preferences, including a living will, and appointing a surrogate decision-maker where applicable. The resident may be encouraged to discuss preferences with loved ones and medical clinicians but should not be pressured to sign a document. Capacity for a particular current decision is assessed separately when needed. Bottom line: Advance-directive notification informs residents about options such as a living will; it does not compel completion.

stem: A 21-year-old patient presents to the emergency department after using marijuana for the first time. The patient reports pounding heart, sweating, fear of dying and shaking. The most appropriate next step would be to administer:
scenario: In the emergency department, a patient becomes frightened, tremulous, and tachycardic after using an unfamiliar cannabis product. The resident obtains vital signs, assesses orientation and chest symptoms, asks about co-ingestants, and provides calm reassurance in a quiet environment. If symptoms remain severe after medical evaluation and supportive measures, lorazepam may provide acute anxiolysis, with observation for clinical improvement. The resident avoids prematurely diagnosing a primary anxiety disorder and gives appropriate harm-reduction counseling before discharge. Escalating confusion, psychosis, chest pain, or abnormal findings require reassessment for alternative causes. Bottom line: Treat severe cannabis-associated panic supportively, adding short-acting benzodiazepine treatment when clinically necessary after medical evaluation.

stem: A 60-year-old patient is brought in by family for a dementia evaluation. The patient is no longer able to feed himself without assistance. On examination, the patient demonstrates bradykinesia, left-sided rigidity, postural instability, and apraxia. The patient frequently raises his left arm into the air, but appears unaware of this action. A brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan is significant for cortical atrophy, greater on the right side than the left. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
scenario: An older adult has progressive loss of independence, severe asymmetric rigidity, apraxia, and reports that one arm moves without intention. The resident documents both cortical and motor findings, obtains collateral history about functional decline and falls, and coordinates neurological assessment rather than attributing the presentation to depression or nonspecific dementia. Care should also address swallowing, mobility, fall risk, caregiver strain, decision-making capacity, and advance planning because management is largely supportive and multidisciplinary. Alien-limb behavior is a neurological sign, not evidence of psychosis. Bottom line: Marked asymmetry with apraxia and alien-limb behavior strongly suggests corticobasal degeneration.

stem: A psychiatrist is asked to see a 62-year-old patient who has been hospitalized after an acute myocardial infarction because staff report that "the patient is driving us crazy." The nurses complain that the patient is constantly requesting information about his condition and treatment, and will refuse tests and medications if he feels the explanations are not sufficient. On interview the patient admits that "I am a perfectionist" but is proud of this fact, saying that it is "the secret of my success." The patient is aware of the staff's frustration, but feels his requests for information are reasonable. Which of the following would be the best advice for the psychiatrist to give the treatment team?
scenario: After an acute myocardial infarction, a patient repeatedly asks staff to explain each medication and test. The consultation resident recommends a consistent communication plan: designate a clinician for regular updates, use plain language, invite questions, and include the patient in medically appropriate choices. The team avoids shaming the patient for wanting detail while setting practical expectations about when updates can occur. If the patient refuses care, clinicians should assess decision-making capacity and clarify misunderstandings before construing the behavior as oppositional. This approach can reduce conflict and help the patient regain an appropriate sense of agency. Bottom line: For reality-based control-seeking patients, structured information-sharing and collaboration are more therapeutic than confrontation.

stem: The parents of an 18-year-old adolescent who is overweight notice that their child is avoiding high caloric foods, such as meat and pasta. When the parents inquire about this, the teen says "I am afraid of eating." The evaluating psychiatrist asks when the eating behavior changed, and the teen reports having had an episode of panic which occurred while eating and was accompanied by choking feelings. A fear of choking while eating and a wish to avoid foods that might cause choking developed. The teen denies other episodes of panic. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
scenario: A clinician evaluates a patient who has progressively narrowed their diet after a choking scare. The assessment includes feared outcomes, avoidance, weight and shape concerns, dysphagia symptoms, medical red flags, nutritional consequences, and whether panic attacks occur unexpectedly outside meals. Once swallowing problems have been appropriately considered, a focused anxiety formulation can guide education and referral for exposure-based psychotherapy. Nutritional or medical clinicians should be involved when intake is substantially affected. Restrictive eating should not automatically be equated with anorexia nervosa, because the feared consequence of eating is diagnostically important. Bottom line: Avoidance of eating because of fear of choking points to a specific phobia when body-image concerns are absent.

stem: A 32-year-old patient with cocaine dependence has been prescribed desipramine by another physician for withdrawal-associated depression. The psychiatrist should warn the patient of which of the following adverse effects that might result from an interaction between desipramine and cocaine?
scenario: A clinician sees a patient using cocaine who reports receiving desipramine elsewhere for depressive symptoms during withdrawal. The clinician reviews recent cocaine use, blood pressure, heart rate, chest symptoms, other medications, and overdose risk, then coordinates medication decisions with the prescriber. The teaching point is not that every co-exposure produces toxicity; combining two agents that enhance norepinephrine signaling can produce clinically important sympathetic and cardiovascular effects. New chest pain, severe headache, neurologic symptoms, or marked hypertension require urgent medical assessment rather than routine psychiatric follow-up. Bottom line: Cocaine plus a norepinephrine-reuptake-blocking tricyclic can dangerously increase blood pressure.

stem: A 54-year-old patient has several days of low grade fever, malaise and severe pain in the right side of the ribcage. Examination reveals an erythematous rash with clusters of tense vesicles, with clear content, on a belt distribution from the front of the chest to the back under the nipple, limited to the right side. Which of the following is the likely causal viral agent?
scenario: A psychiatry clinician on a medical unit evaluates insomnia and distress in a patient with severe burning chest-wall pain. Examination reveals grouped vesicles in a single thoracic dermatome on one side. The clinician recognizes likely zoster and promptly alerts the medical team, since timely medical treatment and infection-control decisions may be relevant. Psychiatric care includes assessing pain-related sleep loss, delirium risk from medications, and emotional distress without attributing severe localized pain to anxiety. Persistent neuropathic pain after rash resolution may require coordinated pain management. Bottom line: A painful unilateral dermatomal vesicular rash is herpes zoster due to varicella zoster virus.

stem: Which of the following statements characterizes late-onset schizophrenia?
scenario: A 62-year-old woman with no prior psychotic disorder develops persistent persecutory ideas and auditory hallucinations. The resident avoids reflexively labeling this as chronic early-onset schizophrenia. The evaluation includes cognitive screening, medication review, sensory impairment, mood symptoms, neurologic history, laboratory assessment as indicated, and collateral history. After secondary causes are considered, the team recognizes that a schizophrenia-spectrum illness can have later onset and that female predominance is characteristic. If medication is indicated, dosing is conservative because older adults have greater adverse-effect vulnerability. Bottom line: New psychosis in later life needs a broad medical evaluation, but late-onset schizophrenia is more common in women.

stem: A first seizure with focal onset and secondary generalization in a 58-year-old patient is most likely the consequence of which of the following?
scenario: A 58-year-old with no seizure history has an episode beginning with left facial twitching and speech arrest, followed by loss of consciousness and generalized convulsions. In the emergency setting, the resident obtains collateral history and helps distinguish seizure semiology from syncope or intoxication. Because focal onset and later age of onset suggest a possible structural cause, urgent neurologic evaluation and brain imaging are prioritized. If imaging identifies a mass, management proceeds with neurology, neurosurgery, and oncology rather than treating the event as uncomplicated alcohol withdrawal. Bottom line: A first focal seizure in later adulthood warrants evaluation for a structural intracranial lesion.

stem: The clock drawing test is a quickly administered and sensitive screen for which of the following disorders?
scenario: During a busy outpatient visit, family members report that a 74-year-old patient is missing bills and getting lost on familiar routes. The resident administers a brief cognitive screen that includes clock drawing and asks the patient to place numbers correctly and set the hands to a specified time. A disorganized clock supports concern for cognitive impairment but does not alone establish dementia. The resident obtains functional history, reviews medications and mood symptoms, assesses for delirium when relevant, and arranges a more complete evaluation. Bottom line: Clock drawing is a quick screen for cognitive impairment and should be integrated with history and formal assessment.

stem: A 65-year-old patient complains of worsening forgetfulness in the context of treatment for life-long depression. The patient undergoes neuropsychological testing to rule out dementia. Which of the following findings would most strongly support a diagnosis of dementia over depression?
scenario: A 65-year-old with chronic depression reports worsening forgetfulness. On testing, the patient is slowed and initially gives up easily but also has persistent difficulty naming familiar objects despite cueing and adequate alertness. The resident recognizes that depression can impair attention and memory performance, yet a focal language-type deficit heightens concern for a neurocognitive disorder. The team gathers collateral history about daily function, reviews medications and medical contributors, assesses mood and delirium, and arranges appropriate follow-up. Bottom line: In a depressed older adult with cognitive complaints, a consistent naming deficit is more concerning for dementia than nonspecific poor concentration.

stem: A 30-year-old patient reports to the psychiatrist being depressed since the death of the patient's mother, 6 months ago. The patient reports being preoccupied at times with thoughts of death and often eats large amounts of sweets to relieve the distress. The patient has gained 15 pounds over the past 2 months. The patient denies anhedonia, and reports that mood often brightens after the patient receives praise at work or when a vacation is upcoming. The patient reports a chronic lack of intimacy, consistently turning down social invitations out of fear of rejection. This patient's symptoms are most consistent with a diagnosis of:
scenario: After a major loss, assessment should explore depressive symptoms rather than equating all sadness with normal bereavement. Useful questions include whether positive events temporarily brighten mood, whether appetite or sleep has increased, whether limbs feel heavy, and whether rejection sensitivity drives withdrawal. The clinician should also assess duration, impairment, suicidal thinking, substance use, prior mania or hypomania, and grief-specific symptoms before assigning a full diagnosis. Mood reactivity during an interview does not rule out clinically significant depression. Treatment planning should address both the depressive syndrome and the interpersonal avoidance that may maintain isolation. Bottom line: Reactive mood with hyperphagia, weight gain, and rejection sensitivity supports atypical depressive features.

stem: A 25-year-old patient is brought to the emergency department after being found in a coma, with an empty bottle of alprazolam next to the patient. The patient is unresponsive and hypotensive. Administration of which of the following substances would be the most effective next step in the management of this patient?
scenario: A patient arrives somnolent after suspected sedative ingestion. The emergency team first addresses airway protection, breathing, circulation, glucose assessment, monitoring, and toxicology consultation as appropriate. If the history strongly supports isolated accidental or iatrogenic benzodiazepine exposure in a patient without dependence, seizure risk, or concerning co-ingestion, flumazenil may be considered. In an unknown intentional overdose, routine antidote administration can be unsafe because withdrawal or seizures may be precipitated. Psychiatric evaluation follows medical stabilization. Bottom line: Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepine effects but is not a routine antidote for every suspected overdose.

stem: A 65-year-old patient is brought to the emergency department with disorientation and mild agitation, and is experiencing vivid visual hallucinations of several children playing inside the house. The patient's family reports that the patient had two similar episodes in recent months, but between them, seemed fine. On examination, the patient has normal language and memory, normal cranial nerves, mild symmetric rigidity and bradykinesia, but no weakness or involuntary movements and no sensory deficits. Deep tendon reflexes are symmetric. A brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan is unremarkable, as are the results of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and routine laboratories including toxic drugs screen. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
scenario: For an older patient who reports seeing people or children in the home, obtain collateral history about timing, cognitive variation, REM sleep behavior, falls, autonomic symptoms, and parkinsonian changes. Review medications and assess for delirium, infection, metabolic disturbance, intoxication, or withdrawal when the presentation is acute. In suspected dementia with Lewy bodies, use dopamine-blocking drugs cautiously because severe sensitivity reactions can occur. A normal bedside memory screen during one visit does not rule out the disorder; longitudinal change and fluctuations matter. Bottom line: Formed visual hallucinations, fluctuating cognition, and spontaneous parkinsonism should prompt consideration of dementia with Lewy bodies.

stem: A 40-year-old patient with a long history of interpersonal difficulties feels socially inept, is sensitive to criticism by others and is reluctant to speak up in almost all social situations. Despite a longing to have a more active social life, the patient has few significant relationships and is regarded by others as timid. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
scenario: When a patient avoids invitations, job interviews, and group participation despite wanting friends or advancement, clarify what drives the avoidance. Ask about fear of negative evaluation, panic-related fear of being unable to escape, lack of interest in intimacy, and reliance on others for decisions. Assess the longitudinal pattern, impairment, temperament, trauma history, and co-occurring social anxiety, depression, or substance use. Treatment should be collaborative and can address avoidance gradually while helping the patient tolerate shame, uncertainty, and anticipated criticism.
